r.summary:
Recommendation: option D (hybrid), with A at its core. Write the widgets once as plain kyo-ui values with no tui4s import, the way examples/widgets/TabsView.scala already is. The web side then uses kyo-ui's own runners (runHandlers on the JVM, runMount on Scala.js) and gives real DOM: native inputs, accessibility, mouse. The terminal side uses tui4s. Layout semantics already match, because tui4s's Layout is "flexbox in cells, following kyo-ui's base CSS", and baseCss makes every element display:flex.

The real gaps are in styling and units, not in layout:
- tui4s maps 1px to 1 cell. In a browser, `padding(1.px)` is one pixel, so the same Style looks broken on the web.
- kyo-ui's Length has no ch, lh or cell variant.
- tui4s ignores Stylesheet, cssClass, Color.Var (it maps it to None), overflow/scroll, position/z-index and mouse. It shows SVG and charts as a 7x1 placeholder.
- kyo-ui's AST is sealed, so a widget cannot be a new node type.

Option B (our own Flutter-style render tree and layout engine with two cell-grid backends) gives the same look on both sides. But it costs about 6-12k LOC (my estimate), throws away the kyo-ui integration and the web-native strengths, and runs into a hard limit: jatatui is JVM-only, so the browser side would need cells streamed from the server or a pure-Scala engine ported to Scala.js. Prior art also points away from B. Flutter web now draws only to a canvas. Compose shares its runtime between Mosaic and Compose web, but the two widget sets are separate. Dioxus deprecated its HTML-to-terminal renderer.

Option C (a terminal in the browser via xterm.js) works today with no code: run ttyd around the launcher script. It is a terminal on the web, not a web app.

Next step: a 1-2 week spike in experiments/dual-target. Port Todo and Dashboard to 6-8 plain-kyo-ui widgets and run them from one JVM with Tui.run and runHandlers. Compare two styling strategies (a build-time target given vs. one UI value with a stylesheet per target). Measure shared vs per-target code, the target branches in each widget, which Style props tui4s ignores, golden and HTML tests, and a ttyd baseline. The exit criteria then pick between widen A, A plus C, or reconsider B.

Network note: WebFetch could not reach any host (DNS failed, and the proxy refused docs.rs with a 403). The claims about other projects therefore come from search result snippets of the pages cited. Version and date facts are marked unverified where the snippets did not confirm them. Facts about tui4s and kyo-ui come from the local sources (paths are given below).

## 1. Prior art (2025-2026)

| Project | How it reaches terminal + web | What it gives up | Lesson for tui4s |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Textual + textual-serve / Textual Web** (Python) | The app runs on a server. textual-serve starts one subprocess per visitor and talks to the browser over a WebSocket with a custom protocol, not a raw shell. Textual Web is the hosted version on a public URL. textual-serve 1.1.3, 2025-11-01. Sources: https://github.com/Textualize/textual-serve, https://pypi.org/project/textual-serve/1.1.0, https://simple-repository.app.cern.ch/project/textual_serve, https://textual.textualize.io/blog/2024/09/08/towards-textual-web-applications/ (2024-09-08; covers links and file downloads in the browser). | The browser shows the terminal rendering, not native web elements. Which front-end renderer it uses (xterm.js?) is unverified. One process per visitor. | Option C, done well: the protocol lets the app ask for web features (links, downloads). Textual CSS has cells as its only absolute unit, plus `fr`, `%`, `w`/`h` and `vw`/`vh` (https://textual.textualize.io/css_types/scalar/). This supports a cell-based token unit. |
| **Ratzilla** (ratatui in the browser via Wasm) | The whole ratatui app compiles to Wasm and runs in the browser. There are three backends: DomBackend (one `<span>` per cell), CanvasBackend, and WebGl2Backend (with a static or dynamic font atlas). It handles mouse and key events and cursor shapes. Sources: https://docs.rs/ratzilla, https://lib.rs/crates/ratzilla (crate updated 2025-04-01), https://gittrend.io/repo/ratatui/ratzilla (last push 2026-04-21). | The web output is a cell grid, not a web app. A11y and text semantics are limited (unverified). It needs the app to compile to Wasm. | This is option B's web backend, already built. For us it cannot run client-side, because jatatui is Java and does not run in Scala.js. |
| **Mosaic** + **Compose Multiplatform web** | Mosaic uses the Compose compiler and runtime for console UI, inspired by Ink; 0.18.0, 2025-08-22, terminal only (https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/jakewharton/mosaic@trunk/README.md, https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/com.jakewharton.mosaic/mosaic-runtime-linuxarm64). Compose Multiplatform web is Kotlin/Wasm on a canvas and reached Beta in 1.9.0, September 2025, with "basic" assistive-technology support (https://blog.jetbrains.com/kotlin/2025/09/compose-multiplatform-1-9-0-compose-for-web-beta/). | The two share the runtime and state model but not the widgets. Mosaic has its own composables, and Compose UI is pixel-based. | Share the state and reactivity layer (Kyo signals, which we already share). The widget layer is the part that needs care. |
| **Redwood** (Cash App) | A widget schema: Compose drives each platform's native toolkit (Android, iOS, web DOM) through per-platform widget implementations (https://code.cash.app/native-ui-and-multiplatform-compose-with-redwood, https://jakewharton.com/native-ui-with-multiplatform-compose/). Current project status is unverified. | Each target needs its own implementation of each widget. | The closest prior art to option A: one widget protocol with per-host implementations. Here the protocol is the kyo-ui AST. |
| **Ink / OpenTUI / Dioxus TUI** | Ink is a React renderer for CLIs, with Yoga flexbox in cells; npm shows 7.x (https://github.com/vadimdemedes/ink, https://socket.dev/npm/package/ink/overview/7.1.0). OpenTUI has a Zig core with Yoga and React and Solid bindings, and OpenCode uses it (https://opentui.com/). Dioxus TUI (rink, later plasmo) rendered the same RSX to the terminal with flexbox. It was deprecated in the Dioxus 0.6 docs, and its README warned that "the ecosystem of widgets is not ready" (https://dioxuslabs.com/learn/0.6/contributing/project_structure, https://docs.rs/plasmo). | Ink shares React but not the host components (Box/Text instead of div). Dioxus TUI did share components, but its widgets never matured. | Dioxus is the warning for A: rendering HTML-like trees to a terminal is easy, but having good widgets on both sides is the real work. Plan the widget library as the product. |
| **Bubble Tea + Wish; ttyd; Zellij web; xterm.js** | Wish is an SSH server (gliderlabs/ssh). Each session gets its own tea.Program with PTY I/O and resize (https://github.com/charmbracelet/wish/blob/2269aa52b64669c0e52e6f61e27643df542d0b50/README.md). ttyd puts any CLI program behind xterm.js, with libwebsockets/libuv, CJK/IME and Sixel (https://man.archlinux.org/man/ttyd.1.en). Zellij 0.43 added a browser client for sessions (https://zellij.dev/news/web-client-multiple-pane-actions/). xterm.js 6.0 added synchronized output (DEC mode 2026) and a WebGL renderer addon (https://newreleases.io/project/npm/@xterm/xterm/release/6.0.0). | These are a terminal on the web. There are no web semantics, and each session costs a process or PTY. | Option C. With ttyd the cost to us is zero today. |
| **Flutter** | Owns its render tree: widgets, then elements, then render objects. Rule: "constraints go down, sizes go up, parent sets position" (https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/layout/constraints, https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/layout/box-constraints). The web output is a canvas only: the HTML renderer was removed in 3.29 and 3.32 in 2025, per secondary sources (https://startdebugging.net/2026/09/canvaskit-vs-skwasm-for-flutter-web-in-2026/). | Owning the engine gives pixel parity, but it means rebuilding text input, accessibility, selection and SEO yourself, and drawing on a canvas. | We can use the layout protocol inside tui4s; measureItem, arrange and place already work that way. Owning the engine is the expensive part to avoid. |
| **Lustre / Elm architecture** | Lustre's "universal components" can run inside an app, as a Web Component, or on the server, where a small client runtime applies DOM patches sent over a WebSocket (https://hexdocs.pm/lustre/lustre.html). Bubble Tea is also an Elm-style architecture. | Web only. | kyo-ui's runHandlers is already this server-push model. The model and update logic do not depend on the target; only the host of the view changes. |

## 2. Design space for tui4s

**(A) Widget / design-system layer that lowers to the kyo-ui AST.**
- *How:* widgets are plain kyo-ui functions. The web uses runHandlers (JVM server push) or runMount (Scala.js). The terminal uses Tui.run.
- *Visual result:* the same structure, tokens and theme on both sides, but not the same pixels. The web looks native, or terminal-like with a theme made for that.
- *Behavior:* the same signals, handlers, onKeyDown shortcuts and Tab order on both sides. tui4s's focusOrder (positive tabIndex in ascending order, then document order) is the same rule as HTML. The web also gets native inputs (IME, selection, clipboard), mouse and accessibility.
- *Hard parts:*
  - Units: tui4s maps 1px to 1 cell; the web uses pixels.
  - Styling: CSS vs terminal attributes. tui4s ignores Stylesheet, cssClass, Var, font size and shadows.
  - Missing in tui4s: scroll (overflow) and overlays (position, z-index). Mouse events are dropped (decision D-30 in EventMapping.scala).
  - Text: line wrapping (tui4s wraps at words) and min-content sizing differ from the browser.
  - Charts: SVG and charts show as a 7x1 placeholder in tui4s.
- *Code (my estimate):*
  - tui4s additions, about 1.5-2.5k LOC: Var resolution plus a stylesheet subset (400-600), scroll (500-800), overlays (300-500), mouse (300).
  - Widget library: 2-4k LOC.
  - Two themes: 300-600 LOC.

**(B) Our own Flutter-style render tree and layout engine with two backends.**
- *How:* a widget, element and render-object tree with cell constraints. One painter writes to a jatatui Buffer; the other draws a cell grid in DOM spans or on a canvas (as Ratzilla does).
- *Visual result:* identical grids on both sides; the web looks like a terminal.
- *Behavior:* identical, with mouse handled by hit-testing cells.
- *Gives up:* native web controls, accessibility, IME and selection, responsive web layout. It also gives up kyo-ui itself, which is tui4s's identity ("a terminal runner for kyo-ui"), and it duplicates the existing 1.9k LOC of Layout, Paint, Props and Geometry.
- *Hard limit:* jatatui is JVM-only. The browser side must either receive cells streamed from the JVM over a WebSocket, which is close to C, or the engine must be pure Scala with no jatatui types so that it cross-builds to Scala.js.
- *Code (my estimate):* 6-12k LOC: engine 3-5k, widgets 2-4k, web client 1-2k, plus text editing.

**(C) Terminal-in-browser streaming of cells to xterm.js.**
- *C0, zero code:* `ttyd examples/target/bin/counter`. Each visitor costs one JVM; startup time and RSS still need to be measured. This works today.
- *C1, in-process:* one tui4s session per WebSocket. It needs a jatatui backend that writes ANSI to a byte sink (it is unverified whether jatatui ships a pure-Java one) and input from the browser. That input is either an ANSI parser (InputPort carries crossterm Events, and the crossterm jar is native) or a thin client that sends key events as JSON. About 0.8-1.5k LOC (my estimate). Caution: TuiApp's capture of System.out and stderr is process-global, so several sessions in one JVM need per-session routing or no capture.
- *Visual and behavior:* the same as the terminal, because it is a terminal. It gives up everything web-native.

**(D) Hybrid (recommended).**
- A is the main path: widgets written once, the web via kyo-ui runners, the terminal via tui4s.
- A second web theme makes the browser look like a terminal on purpose.
- C0 is documented now as "terminal in the browser"; C1 comes later only if people ask for it.
- B is not built. Its constraint protocol can be used inside tui4s's Layout.
- Cost: A plus about 0-1.5k LOC.

## 3. What exists on main, and what kyo-ui's Style can express

**tui4s core today** (`modules/core/src/main`, about 7.3k LOC):
- Layout.scala: "flexbox in cells, following kyo-ui's base CSS (everything is flex, reactive boundaries are transparent)". It measures (measureItem and measureElement against the available width), arranges, then places nodes into an immutable flat index (`Laid`), repaints by damage, and relays out a single container.
- kyo-ui's HtmlRenderer.baseCss sets `div, p, ul, h1… { display:flex; flex-direction:column }` and `nav, li, span, button, a { display:flex; flex-direction:row; align-items:center }`. tui4s's Props.defaultDir follows this rule exactly.
- The model is already Flutter-like: the available width goes down, natural sizes come up, and the parent sets the rect. This makes **A the natural fit**: the web runner and tui4s already agree on flex semantics.
- examples/widgets/TabsView.scala is already a plain kyo-ui widget with no tui4s import. Tabs.scala adds the tui4s mount lifetime.
- tui4s components (ComponentSpec.node) are a kyo-ui `Reactive` kept in a registry. The code says "Another kyo-ui runner sees `fallback`". So widgets must not depend on tui4s Component or hooks if they are to run on the web.

**Props.applyStyle supports:** bg and text color (Hex, Rgb, and Rgba only when alpha ≥ 0.5), padding, margin, gap, flex direction (including reverse), align, alignSelf, justify, width, height, min and max sizes, grow, shrink, font weight (bold), italic, underline and strike, text transform, text align, opacity below 0.7 (shown as dim), list style, hidden, border width (capped at 1 cell), style (solid, dashed, dotted, none), color, and radius (shown as rounded glyphs).

**tui4s ignores:**
- Stylesheet and cssClass (tui4s never reads them).
- `Color.Var`, which falls to `case _ => None`.
- Length.Calc and Auto, which give no fixed size.
- Overflow, position, z-index, flex-wrap, font size, line height, shadows, transitions, animations, filters and gradients.
- Mouse events.
- SVG, which shows as a 7x1 placeholder in Layout.intrinsic.

**kyo-ui Style CAN express** (sources: `.../kyo-src/kyo-ui/kyo/Style.scala`, `Stylesheet.scala`, `Length.scala`):
- Everything flex, plus pseudo-states (hover, focus, active, disabled).
- `cssClass` and `.data(name, value)` attributes.
- `Stylesheet` with rule, media (including `MediaQuery.raw`, `prefersDark`, min and max width), `vars`, `scopedVars(selector, …)`, `fontFace` and keyframes.
- `Color.variable(name)`, rendered as `var(--name)`.
- `FontFamily.Monospace`.
- `PageHead.css`, raw CSS emitted after baseCss.

That is enough for:
1. **A terminal theme mapped to CSS variables.** One Scala `Theme` (token to color) renders to `Stylesheet.vars(...)` for the web and to a palette map for tui4s, once tui4s resolves `Var`. ANSI-named tokens (for example `ansi-blue`) can map to jatatui's indexed colors, so the terminal follows the user's own colour scheme, while the web gets an xterm-like palette.
2. **A monospace web theme that looks like the terminal on purpose.** Raw CSS in PageHead.css can set a monospace font, a fixed line-height, and cell sizes in `ch` (horizontal) and `lh` (vertical). `lh` is supported in Chrome 109+, Firefox 120+ and Safari 16.4+ (https://caniuse.com/mdn-css_types_length_lh, https://webkit.org/blog/16831/line-height-units/).
3. **A "cells" unit as a design token.** Widgets use `Space(n)` and never raw px. On the terminal this is n px, which tui4s draws as n cells. On the web it is either n × cell width or n × cell height in px, taken from font metrics, or a class whose raw CSS uses ch and lh.

**kyo-ui Style CANNOT express:**
- A `ch`, `lh` or cell `Length`. The variants are only Px, Pct, Em, Vh, Calc and Auto.
- A Length taken from a variable, even though the Stylesheet Scaladoc mentions "Length's variable form". There is no such variant in RC7's Length.scala, so the docs and the code disagree.
- Calc for padding or gap: these are typed `Px | Pct | Em` and `Px | Em`.
- Terminal-only attributes: ANSI-indexed colors, reverse video, blink, double or heavy border glyph sets.
- A media condition that means "the terminal is the target". A possible hack: `MediaQuery.raw("(-tui4s-terminal)")`, which tui4s would treat as true and browsers should evaluate as false (an unknown media feature, per Media Queries 4; unverified across browsers).
- New AST node types: the AST is sealed. Terminal-specific widgets must lower to div, span and table plus classes, `data-*` hints or Unicode text (block characters for gauges). Charts need a subset of SVG drawn into a braille canvas in tui4s (a later phase).

## 4. Spike: "one widget source, two hosts" (1-2 weeks)

**Where:** `experiments/dual-target/` with its own build, like `experiments/ui-state/frame`. Not published. It depends on tui4s core, kyo-ui and kyo-http. tui4s core changes go on an experiment branch only.

**Week 1**
- D1: Theme and tokens. Build two styling strategies on two widgets (Panel, Button) and compare:
  - S1, build-time target: a `given Target`; widgets produce different Styles per host.
  - S2, one UI value for both hosts: `cssClass` plus a stylesheet per target. This needs a minimal class/tag/`:focus` selector resolver and `Var` resolution in tui4s.
- D2-D4: six to eight widgets in plain kyo-ui, in a module that has no tui4s dependency (this is the compile-time check): Panel (border and title), Button, TextField, List/Select (arrow-key navigation, a selection signal), Tabs (from TabsView), Table, Gauge (Unicode block text), KeyHints/StatusBar.
- D5: one `main` that runs `Tui.run(app)` in the terminal and `runHandlers("/app")(app)` on localhost in the same JVM. Stretch: SignalRefs created outside the by-name block, so the terminal and the browser show one live state.

**Week 2**
- D6-D7: port Todo and Dashboard so that they use only the widget module.
- D8: on the probe branch, add the tui4s pieces S2 needs and count their LOC.
- D9: a web "terminal look" theme (monospace, ch and lh through PageHead.css) next to a "web native" theme. Take screenshots.
- D10: the ttyd baseline (C0): time to first frame and RSS per session. Write the go/no-go note.

**What to measure**
- Shared vs per-target lines of widget code. Target: at least 90% shared, with per-target code only in theme files.
- `Target` branches in each widget. Target: at most 1, ideally 0.
- The kyo-ui Style props the widgets use that tui4s ignores. This list becomes the tui4s backlog, with a LOC estimate for each.
- Tests: each widget has an 80x24 golden test on `tui4s.testkit.Headless` and a `UI.runRender` HTML snapshot, and both are green.
- Keyboard parity: the same key script gives the same signal states in Headless. In the browser, a manual check of Tab, arrows, Enter, Space and Esc.
- Performance: tui4s FrameStats frame time stays the same; WebSocket bytes per keypress on the web.
- Every layout difference found (wrapping, min-content, rounding of percentages) and every kyo-ui gap found. These become upstream asks: a cell, ch or lh Length; a Length variable; a documented hook for host hints.

**Exit criteria**
- **GO (widen A/D):** two apps and at least six widgets run in both hosts from one source; at most one target branch per widget; the widget module has no tui4s import; the tui4s gaps come to about five items or fewer, each with an estimate; the web app works keyboard-only and with the mouse; a theme change is one value.
- **PIVOT:** if more than about 30% of widget lines branch per target, or layout differences make two or more widgets unusable on one host, keep A for forms and layout widgets and use C1 for a "web terminal" mode. Reconsider B only if the user says the web must be identical to the terminal grid.
- **STOP/rethink:** if one JVM cannot host Tui.run and runHandlers together, because of the global output capture, the scheduler knobs, or tui4s's one-fiber drawing rule.

**How this relates to the widget library ("enough widgets for most terminal apps")**
- The spike's widgets are the seed of a widgets module. Proposal: `modules/widgets` with its own release tag. It can be cross-built for JVM and JS, since it depends only on kyo-ui, and it never imports tui4s.
- tui4s adds only the terminal host and the terminal theme. The web adds only a web theme.
- Each widget is offered in two forms: controlled (signals passed in, with an `onChange`) and uncontrolled (it makes its own state at construction, as TabsView does). Mount lifetime stays an optional tui4s wrapper (as Tabs.scala does).
- Each widget is tested twice: Headless golden and runRender snapshot.
- Roster after the spike: Text/Paragraph, Panel, Row/Column/Stack/Spacer/Split, Button, TextField/TextArea, Checkbox/Radio/Switch, Select/List, Tabs, Table (scroll, sort), Tree, Gauge/Progress, Spinner, Sparkline/Chart (a subset of SVG drawn to braille in tui4s), ScrollView, Modal/Popover/Toast, StatusBar/KeyHints/Help, Command palette, Log view.
- The ScrollView and overlay widgets are what bring scroll and overlay support into tui4s core.
- A `.vue`-like template or JSX syntax for Scala ("scalax") should be a front end that compiles to these same widget calls, not a separate renderer. That is a separate spike.

options.name: A: widget/design-system layer that lowers to the kyo-ui AST
options.how: Widgets are plain kyo-ui functions with no tui4s import. The web uses kyo-ui's runHandlers (JVM server push) or runMount (Scala.js); the terminal uses Tui.run. Units are cell tokens; a theme value renders to Stylesheet.vars for the web and to a palette for tui4s. tui4s learns Color.Var, a class/tag/:focus stylesheet subset, scroll, overlays and mouse.
options.pros: Fits main: tui4s Layout already follows kyo-ui baseCss, so flex semantics match the web. Keeps tui4s's identity as a kyo-ui runner. The web gets native inputs, accessibility, IME, selection, mouse and responsive layout. The same signals and handlers run on both sides. TabsView already shows the pattern.
options.cons: The same UI does not give the same pixels. Units differ (tui4s maps 1px to 1 cell), and kyo-ui has no ch, lh or cell Length and no Length variable. tui4s ignores Stylesheet, cssClass, Var, overflow, position, z-index and mouse, and shows SVG as a 7x1 placeholder. The AST is sealed, so there are no custom widget nodes. Text wrapping and min-content sizes differ. Dioxus TUI shows that the widgets, not the renderer, are the hard part.
options.cost: My estimate: tui4s additions about 1.5-2.5k LOC, widget library 2-4k LOC, two themes 300-600 LOC. The spike is 1-2 weeks.

options.name: B: own Flutter-style render tree and layout engine with two backends
options.how: A widget, element and render-object tree with cell constraints (constraints down, sizes up, parent positions). One painter writes to a jatatui Buffer; a second draws a cell grid in DOM spans or on a canvas, like Ratzilla.
options.pros: Identical look and behavior on both sides. Full control. Mouse hit-testing is easy in a cell grid.
options.cons: Duplicates the existing Layout, Paint and Props code (1.9k LOC) and drops kyo-ui, which is tui4s's identity. Gives up web-native controls, accessibility, IME and selection. jatatui is JVM-only, so the browser either gets cells streamed from the server or the engine must be pure Scala and cross-built to Scala.js. Flutter web is canvas-only, and Compose kept separate widget sets for terminal and web: owning the engine is costly.
options.cost: My estimate: 6-12k LOC (engine 3-5k, widgets 2-4k, web client 1-2k, plus text editing). Several months.

options.name: C: terminal in the browser (cells streamed to xterm.js)
options.how: C0: wrap the existing launcher script in ttyd (or Zellij web, or Wish over SSH). C1: one tui4s session per WebSocket in the same JVM, with an ANSI output backend and input from the browser (an ANSI parser, or a thin client that sends JSON key events) feeding an InputPort.
options.pros: C0 works today with zero code. Terminal and web look and behave the same, because it is a terminal. Mature prior art: ttyd, textual-serve, Zellij 0.43, xterm.js 6.
options.cons: A terminal on the web, not a web app: no DOM semantics, accessibility or responsive layout. C0 costs one JVM per visitor. For C1, it is unverified whether jatatui has a pure-Java ANSI backend; the crossterm input path is native; TuiApp's output capture is process-global, which conflicts with many sessions in one JVM.
options.cost: C0: 0 LOC plus a docs page. C1: about 0.8-1.5k LOC (my estimate), 1-2 weeks.

options.name: D: hybrid (A core + web-terminal theme + C0 now, C1 later)
options.how: A is the main path. A second web theme (monospace, ch and lh via PageHead.css) makes the browser look like the terminal on purpose. C0 is documented now; C1 is built only on demand. B's constraint protocol is used inside tui4s Layout instead of as a new engine.
options.pros: Covers both meanings of 'works in both': a native web app and a terminal look on the web. Builds on what exists. The steps can be shipped one by one.
options.cons: Two themes to maintain. Still has all of A's style and unit gaps. The 'terminal look' web theme only approximates the grid (CSS borders are not box-drawing glyphs).

recommendations: Choose D with A as the core: widgets are written once in plain kyo-ui (no tui4s import); the web uses kyo-ui runners (runHandlers on the JVM, runMount on Scala.js); the terminal uses tui4s. Do not build a separate render engine (B) now.

Run the 1-2 week spike in experiments/dual-target (own build, not published): 6-8 widgets, Todo and Dashboard, one JVM that runs Tui.run and runHandlers, two styling strategies compared (S1 build-time target vs S2 one UI value with per-target stylesheets).
Unit rule for widget code: use cell tokens (Space(n)), never raw px. tui4s keeps 1px = 1 cell; the web theme turns a cell into ch/lh via PageHead.css, or into px from known font metrics.

One Theme value as the single source for colors: it renders to Stylesheet.vars for the web and to a tui4s palette. tui4s must resolve Color.Var (today it maps it to None), and ANSI-named tokens should map to indexed colors so the terminal keeps the user's colour scheme.

Turn the spike's list of 'Style props tui4s ignores' into separate tui4s PRs: Var resolution, a cssClass/Stylesheet subset (class, tag, data, :focus), overflow scroll, overlays (position, z-index), mouse (this revisits D-30). Each PR needs its own compat note.
Test every widget on both hosts: a tui4s.testkit.Headless golden at 80x24 and a UI.runRender HTML snapshot.
Document C0 (ttyd around the launcher script) now as the zero-code 'terminal in the browser'. Defer C1, and note before C1 that TuiApp's output capture is process-global.

Take the gaps to kyo-ui upstream: a cell, ch or lh Length; a Length variable (the Stylesheet Scaladoc mentions one, but RC7's Length has none); a documented extension point or data-* convention for host-specific hints, since the AST is sealed.
openQuestions: Which web look does the user want: native web, a terminal look on purpose, or both themes? This decides how much weight A and B get.

Must the web version run client-side (Scala.js runMount, static hosting) or is server push (runHandlers, a JVM server, state per connection) acceptable? tui4s itself can never run in the browser, because jatatui is JVM-only.
Should the terminal and the browser show one live shared state (one app, two views) or be separate deployments?
Is mouse support in the terminal in scope (it reverses decision D-30)?
Where does the widget module live: modules/widgets in the tui4s repo with its own release tag, or a separate repo? What is its name, and is it cross-built for JVM and JS?
Will the kyo-ui maintainers take upstream changes (cell, ch or lh units; a Length variable; a host-hint hook)? Is a local workaround acceptable until then?
What accessibility level is required on the web?
Should the '.vue for Scala' / JSX ('scalax') spike come after this one as a front end over the same widget layer?

Unverified facts to check before deciding: whether jatatui has a pure-Java ANSI backend (this sets C1's cost); textual-serve's browser renderer; Redwood's maintenance status; Ratzilla's current version.

r.summary:
Recommendation: do not revive XML literals. Option (c) is a dead end: the Scala 3 reference says XML literals "will be dropped", `-source:future` already rejects them, and the planned replacement interpolator is unmaintained.

Spike option (a): a `ui"..."` / `ui"""..."""` interpolator, written as a Scala 3 quotes macro. At compile time it parses the literal and expands it into ordinary kyo-ui builder calls. Because the output is a plain kyo-ui value, the same template runs on all four runners (DOM mount, server push, HTML stream, tui4s terminal) and needs no tui4s internals. That is the "works in both terminal and web" property the user wants. The macro APIs it needs all exist: StringContext/Varargs, quotes.reflect, Position.apply(sourceFile, start, end) and report.error/errorAndAbort. The Scala compiler's own `f` interpolator and the Binding.scala/html.scala 3.x `html"""..."""` interpolator are working precedents.

Main known limit: each hole is typed on its own, before the macro runs, against `Any`. So a lambda hole without parameter types (`v => ref.set(v)`) does not compile, and TSX-style contextual typing is not possible. By-name handlers stay lazy because the arguments are `inline`.

Keep option (d), the existing builder DSL, as the baseline. It is already close to JSX in structure (`div(h1("Counter"), button("+").onClick(inc))`) and has full IDE support.

Defer option (b), a .vue-like single-file component. It is the only option that lets a template bind names (v-for). But a good IDE experience would need a language server, as Vue (Volar) and Svelte (svelte2tsx) did, and Twirl shows the cost of not having one.

Run the spike after the core widget work: the vocabulary of tags, attributes and component tags has to be stable first. Put it in a separate build under experiments/, outside the root build.sbt, so no published module becomes unreleased.

Two local facts limit (b)'s style block. tui4s ignores kyo-ui `Stylesheet`/`cssClass` (it reads only inline `Style`). It also paints SVG as a 7x1 placeholder and Img as `[alt]`. So any style block must lower to inline `Style` values.

WebFetch could not reach any host from this sandbox. Most claims below come from search-result snippets, and they are marked "unverified" where I could not confirm them.

So document-level CSS rules do not reach the terminal; only inline `Style` does. Any template layer that emits only kyo-ui public builder calls therefore works on all runners. options.name: (a) ui"..." macro string interpolator
options.how: Inline extension on StringContext with inline args: Any*. A quotes.reflect macro reads the raw parts (Varargs), parses the HTML-like syntax, checks hole types (TypeRepr <:<, Expr.summon[AsHtmlChild[T]]), reports errors at Position(sourceFile, partStart+offset, ...) with report.error / errorAndAbort, and emits kyo-ui builder calls (UI.div.apply(...).onClick(hole)).
options.pros: Full type safety, because the output is ordinary kyo-ui code. Works on all four runners (DOM, server push, HTML stream, tui4s terminal) and on Scala.js, because the macro runs at compile time on the JVM. By-name handlers stay lazy (inline args). Holes are plain Scala (Metals has interpolation completions since 0.11.8). Precedents: html.scala 3.x html""" interpolator and the compiler's f interpolator (partError at an offset). One small library module.
options.cons: Holes are typed against Any before expansion, so lambda holes need parameter types (no TSX-like contextual typing). Templates cannot bind names (no v-for); use a nested ui in a lambda hole, JSX style. Errors in generated glue land at the call site unless the macro pre-validates. No completion or highlighting inside the literal without an injection grammar. Holes are ${} rather than JSX {}. A per-call-site parse cost. Tracks the kyo-ui element set.
options.cost: Spike 5 days; productize 3-5 weeks plus about 2 days for a VS Code/tree-sitter injection grammar; medium maintenance (lower if attributes are resolved by reflection).

options.name: (b) .scalax/.sui single-file component with an sbt generator (Twirl/Vue-like)
options.how: A file with <script lang="scala">, <template> and <style> blocks. An sbt sourceGenerators task (plus Mill/scala-cli equivalents) writes one .scala per component: the script body, then the template lowered to kyo-ui builders (or to ui""" calls). Positions are mapped back to the .scalax file (Twirl-style, via sbt sourcePositionMappers; unverified). The style block lowers to inline kyo Style values.
options.pros: The only option where templates can bind names (for/v-for, slot props) and script and template share scope without wrapping. Familiar to Vue users. Output is still plain kyo-ui, so both targets work. Generated code is fully type-checked.
options.cons: IDE support inside .scalax needs a language server (Vue needed Volar/vue-tsc, Svelte needed svelte2tsx). Without one there is no completion, and go-to-definition lands in target/ generated code; Twirl's lack of tooling and slow compiles are known pains. Several build-tool plugins. A CSS <style> block would not render in the terminal, because tui4s reads only inline Style (no Stylesheet/cssClass), so the block must be Scala Style values or a CSS subset mapped to Style.
options.cost: 4-8 weeks without a language server, months with one; high maintenance.

options.name: (c) Revive XML literal syntax
options.how:
Use Scala 3's remaining XML-literal parser (
{x}
) with scala-xml or a shadow scala.xml package, or a compiler plugin that retargets the desugaring to kyo-ui (like the Scala 2 NameBasedXml / Binding.scala approach).
options.pros: Real markup in Scala source, and the IDEs parse it today. Quick to demo.
options.cons: Dead end. The Scala 3 reference says XML literals will be dropped in favour of an XML string interpolator. -source:future already rejects them (Scala 3.4-era forum report). The replacement xml-interpolator is unmaintained. The name-based XML SIP is on hold. scala-xml nodes are untyped, so retargeting needs a hack. Binding.scala itself moved to an html""" interpolator for Scala 3.
options.cost: 1-2 weeks for a hack with a high risk of breaking on a future Scala version; not recommended.

options.name: (d) Improve the existing kyo-ui builder DSL
options.how: Keep div(h1("x"), button("+").onClick(inc)). Add small ergonomics, for example auto-lifting Signal[Int] (or Signal of a Show type) children, which today need .map(_.toString). Document the rule that Signal setters come last. Propose upstream kyo-ui changes where they belong, rather than adding a tui4s syntax layer.
options.pros: Already close to JSX in structure and fully typed, with content-model checks (ul accepts only li, no SVG primitive in HTML). Perfect IDE support. Zero build cost. Runner-neutral by construction.
options.cons: Not markup: parentheses instead of closing tags, and attributes as chained setters after the factory. Signal-typed setters return UI, so ordering matters. Implicit-search errors (AsHtmlChild) can be cryptic. Most real fixes belong upstream in kyo-ui, not in tui4s.
options.cost: Days; low maintenance. This is also the baseline the spike is measured against.

recommendations: Do not revive XML literals (option c). Scala 3 plans to drop them, -source:future rejects them, and the planned replacement interpolator is unmaintained.

Keep the kyo-ui builder DSL (option d) as the main API and the baseline. It is already structurally close to JSX and fully supported by the IDEs. Send small ergonomic gaps (for example Signal[Int] children) upstream to kyo-ui rather than building a tui4s syntax layer.

Spike option (a), a `ui"""..."""` Scala 3 macro interpolator that emits only kyo-ui public builder calls. That keeps it runner-neutral: the same template runs in the terminal (tui4s) and on the web (DOM mount, server push, HTML stream).
Schedule the spike after the core widget work. The template vocabulary (elements tui4s renders well, and widget/component tags) and the component API (Hooks, Component) must be stable first.

Put the spike in experiments/scalax with its own sbt build (two subprojects: macro and use), outside the root build.sbt, so no published module becomes unreleased. Timebox it to 5 days. Use the exit criteria in the details: same Headless screen and runRender HTML as the DSL Counter and Todo; at least 8 positioned negative cases asserted with typeCheckErrors; lazy handlers; compile time no more than 2x the DSL; an IDE matrix for Metals and IntelliJ.

Read the html.scala 3.x / Binding.scala 12.2 interpolator source and the compiler's f-interpolator macro (per-part offset errors) before writing the parser. They are the two closest working precedents.

In the macro, pre-validate everything a user can get wrong and report it at Position(sourceFile, partStart + offset, ...). Do not let kyo-ui implicit-search errors surface at the call site. Return type UI, not transparent inline, for IntelliJ.

If a single-file component (option b) is ever built, layer it on the (a) parser, and lower any style block to inline kyo Style values: tui4s ignores Stylesheet and cssClass. Do not start it before (a) passes, and budget for a language server or accept Twirl-level tooling.
openQuestions: Should the template only cover kyo-ui elements, or also tui4s components as uppercase tags (<Tabs selected=${s}/>)? The second ties the spike to the Component/Hooks API.
Is a template layer a tui4s artifact at all? Its output is runner-neutral kyo-ui, so it may fit better upstream in kyo or in a separate repo (like pini4s).
Which IDE matters most to the user: Metals/VS Code or IntelliJ? That decides whether the effort goes to a TextMate/tree-sitter injection grammar or to IntelliJ language-injection guidance.
Is ${...} hole syntax (instead of JSX {...}) and $$ for a literal dollar acceptable to the user, or is real JSX brace syntax a hard requirement? A hard requirement would push toward option (b).
What compile-time overhead is acceptable for the go threshold (I proposed no more than 2x the DSL for 50 templates)?
Unverified: whether Scala 3.9.0 still parses XML literals by default. I could not open the 3.9 reference page; the 3.7.2 page says 'still supported, but will be dropped'.
Unverified: whether quotes.reflect can attach source positions to synthesized trees, so that errors in generated glue point inside the literal. If it cannot, the macro must pre-validate everything.
Unverified: exact part-offset behaviour for single- vs triple-quoted (and any new dedented) literals in 3.9 (scala/scala3 PR 24185). The spike must test both forms.
Should whitespace between tags follow JSX trimming rules or HTML rules? It matters more in the terminal, where a stray space costs a cell.
